setupSteps: Pulley height: set the pulley to its highest notch (Rep Fitness, Masterclass, Bodybuilding.com).
Attachment: clip on a rope attachment and check the clip is closed.
Weight: pick a light weight on the stack; check the pin is fully in.
Knee pad: put a mat or folded towel under your knees if the floor is hard.
Distance: kneel about 30-60 cm back from the stack, facing it, knees hip-width apart (distance is an est.; sources say "a foot or two").

Hands: hold the rope ends with both hands and bring them beside your face or against your forehead, elbows pointing down. Do not hold the rope behind your neck for your first sessions; it makes the neck pull easy to do.
Hips: sit your hips slightly back but keep them above your heels; your thighs should stay roughly upright, not sitting on your heels.
Spotter: not needed for light weight.

Seat height: release the pin and set the seat so the machine's pivot is roughly level with your lower ribs or mid-torso (Legion Athletics; the Hoist HD-3600 manual describes changing the seat with a pull pin). Machines differ, so read the label.

Pads and handles: the chest or shoulder pad should sit on the upper chest below the collarbone, handles at a comfortable reach; hands or elbows only hold on. Foot rollers or shin pads, where fitted, keep the hips still.
Back: sit all the way back with your lower back against the pad, knees about 90 degrees (est.).
Weight: pin the lightest stack that lets you do 12 slow reps; ask staff to check the first time.

steps.title: Get into position
steps.action: Kneel at the cable (or sit on the machine) with the rope beside your face (or hands on the handles), back long and chest tall.
steps.visualCheck: Side: head over shoulders, shoulders over hips, thighs about upright. Front: elbows level, knees hip-width apart.

steps.title: Set the neck and arms
steps.action: Lock the rope beside your face, elbows pointing down; keep your arms still and do not pull with them.
steps.feel: Light hold in the hands, no neck strain.
steps.visualCheck: Side: rope does not move relative to the head. Front: elbows even.

steps.title: Brace the abdomen
steps.action: Tighten the belly as if preparing to cough and keep the hips still.
steps.feel: Belly firm, no arch in the lower back.
steps.breathing: Breathe in, then out as you start.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs level with the pelvis (not flared out).

steps.title: Curl the ribs toward the hips
steps.action: Bend the spine forward, bringing your elbows toward your thighs, shortening the distance between ribs and pelvis. Hips stay where they are.
steps.feel: Abs squeezing; not the arms or the neck.
steps.visualCheck: Side: the upper back rounds slightly and the trunk bends forward; the hips do not move toward your heels.

steps.title: Squeeze at the end
steps.action: Stop when your elbows are near your thighs or knees; do not sit back onto your heels.
steps.visualCheck: Side: trunk angle (shoulder-hip-knee) about 110 degrees or less (est.); hips still.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Return slowly to upright by straightening the spine, taking at least as long as the lift.
steps.visualCheck: Side: the weight stack moves smoothly; no bounce.

steps.title: Stop at upright, not arched
steps.action: At the top stop with the trunk upright and the back straight; do not let the weight pull you into a back arch.
steps.breathing: Breathe in, then out as you lift again.
steps.visualCheck: Side: trunk angle about 150 degrees or more but not past about 180 (est.).

steps.title: Finish
steps.action: After the last rep, lower the stack until it rests, release the rope, and stand up slowly.
steps.visualCheck: Weight stack is resting before you let go.

commonMistakes.title: Moving the hips
commonMistakes.text: Moving the hips. Why: the hips take over, making it a hip-flexor exercise and increasing the chance of lower back strain (coaching sources). Fix: lock the hips and only curl the spine.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling with the arms
commonMistakes.text: Pulling with the arms. Why: the arms pull the rope down, which reduces the work for the abs and can strain the neck. Fix: lighter weight, hold the rope beside the face and let the arms stay still.

commonMistakes.title: Going too heavy
commonMistakes.text: Going too heavy. Why: leads to back, neck or disc strain in coaching guidance and to swinging. Fix: use a weight you can lower for 3 seconds for 10-12 reps with 2-3 reps in reserve.

commonMistakes.title: Using a short range of motion
commonMistakes.text: Using a short range of motion. Why: the abs do not shorten fully (one coaching guide notes many people use a restricted range). Fix: curl until the elbows approach the thighs.

commonMistakes.title: Arching the back at the start
commonMistakes.text: Arching the back at the start. Why: lets the weight pull the lower back into extension under load. Fix: start upright with the ribs level to the pelvis.

commonMistakes.title: Sitting back on the heels
commonMistakes.text: Sitting back on the heels. Why: the thighs and hips move instead of the spine. Fix: keep the hips above the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Rushing and bouncing
commonMistakes.text: Rushing and bouncing. Why: momentum replaces muscle work. Fix: 2 seconds up, 1 pause, 3 seconds down.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: can raise blood pressure briefly. Fix: breathe out as you curl.

commonMistakes.title: Machine: pushing with the arms or feet instead of curling
commonMistakes.text: Machine: pushing with the arms or feet instead of curling. Why: reduces the abs' share. Fix: hold lightly and curl the ribs to the pelvis.

commonMistakes.title: Doing it every day
commonMistakes.text: Doing it every day. Why: recovery. Fix: 2-3 sessions per week with a rest day between (est.).

safetyNotes: Loaded spinal flexion: the exercise repeatedly bends the spine under load. Laboratory and modelling work (McGill and colleagues) links this to disc stress; a 2011 NSCA review (Contreras and Schoenfeld) says the idea of a limited number of bending cycles is an assumption and that evidence in living people is limited. Beginners should keep the weight light, move slowly and stop if the lower back hurts.
Neck: pulling the rope into the neck can strain it; keep the rope beside the face and the arms still.
Hip flexor and lower back: small surface-EMG studies found high rectus femoris activity during machine crunches and caution for people with lower back problems; no cable crunch study was found.
Osteoporosis: consensus guidance advises avoiding forward spine bending under load; this exercise is an avoid for most people with low bone mass or a spine fracture (see table).
Pregnancy and postpartum: advice conflicts (some trainers say avoid crunches, one 2015 study reported narrowing of the gap with crunches); ask an obstetrician or pelvic health physiotherapist.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure.
Spotter: not needed. Machine: ask staff to check the first time.
Equipment check: check the rope clip, the stack pin, the pulley height lock, and on the machine the seat pin and pad bolts.
Gym etiquette: wipe the pads and handles, return the rope, reset the pulley, do not hog the station between sets, ask staff before filming and do not film other members.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); many are coaching blogs. The 150/110 degree trunk thresholds, 70 degree knee limit, 3 s minimum rep, sets, reps, rest, tempo and starting-weight steps are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: an ACSM, ACE (beyond the seated crunch listing), NSCA, NHS, Mayo Clinic or Harvard Health cable-crunch page or prescription; EMG data for the cable crunch itself; the ExRx muscle lists for the cable crunch; a standard cable-crunch hand position; a controlled trial of ab rep ranges; condition-specific sources for knee pain, shoulder problems, obesity, PCOS and lower back pain with cable or machine crunches.
